passage: I am Damini, and this is how I stopped feeling behind. Before boards my head was one big fog: everything was undone, so nothing felt done. One evening I took a fresh notebook and gave each subject its own page. Under Maths: chapters one to fifteen, each with a small box, then five past-paper sets and one formula sheet. Same for Science and the rest. Every night before dinner I ticked whatever I had finished. On hopeless days I simply counted the ticks. Vikas, who sits behind me in class, once peeked and said, "That is oddly satisfying." It was. The syllabus had not changed, but now I could see where I stood.

qa.a: Damini listed chapters with small boxes, past-paper sets and a formula sheet.

qa.a: Overwhelmed and behind, since everything felt undone and so nothing felt done.

qa.a: As oddly satisfying, since Vikas said so on peeking, which suggests it looks clear and motivating.

Counsellor's note, 8 January — Elizabeth, Class 12
Elizabeth came in on 18 December saying she felt "behind in everything" but couldn't say where. I asked her to give each subject its own page: every chapter, every past-paper set, every formula sheet, each with an empty box beside it. Physics alone ran to two pages, and she looked alarmed. Today she brought the pages back. Each night she ticks what she has finished; Chemistry is about half ticked, Physics a third, and she has pencilled dates next to the gaps. She said, "I still have loads left, but now I can see how much loads is." She looked less pale than in December. We agreed she will bring the sheets every fortnight, and I will ask about sleep too.
— Ankita, school counsellor

qa.q: How much of Chemistry had Elizabeth ticked?
What was Elizabeth feeling when she said she was behind in everything?
qa.a: She felt anxious and overwhelmed by a vague sense of being behind, without knowing where the gaps actually were.

qa.q: What else could make Elizabeth's lists more useful?
qa.a: Marking which unticked items carry the most marks, so each night's ticks go to the chapters that matter most first.

qa.q: How does Ankita see Elizabeth's progress?
qa.a: Ankita notices Elizabeth looks less pale and can now see what is left, and plans fortnightly check-ins that include sleep.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a student turning subjects into checklists and ticking items nightly so progress becomes visible.

Wednesday, 11:40 pm
Ticked off three things tonight: Biology chapter 6, the 2019 Chemistry paper and my trig formula sheet. That's 41 ticks out of 112 across all five subjects. Two weeks ago I'd have said I was "hopelessly behind", and I couldn't have told you behind in what. Now it's all written on five sheets stuck inside my cupboard door, one per subject, chapter by chapter, with boxes. Jyoti laughed at the sheets and called them my "wall of doom". Maybe. But the doom has boxes now, and 41 of them are ticked. English is nearly done, which means I can steal some English evenings for Physics, the scary one. Going to sleep before midnight for once.
— Ramesh

qa.q: How many ticks does Ramesh have so far?
qa.a: 41 ticks out of 112 across all five subjects.

qa.q: How does Ramesh feel about the lists compared with two weeks ago?
qa.a: Ramesh feels calmer and more in control; two weeks ago there was only a vague, hopeless feeling of being behind.

qa.q: What would you advise Ramesh to do with the spare English evenings?
qa.a: Give them to Physics as planned, and put a Physics item in each night's target so the scary subject shrinks steadily.

qa.q: What might the sheets look like to Jyoti?
qa.a: To Jyoti they look like a funny, gloomy "wall of doom", without seeing that the boxes are what make Ramesh feel less doomed 😅.

grounding: A student's diary shows chapter-by-chapter checklists ticked nightly turning a vague feeling of being behind into visible progress.
